analysis.one_liner: Would fund zero-carbon school buildings and dramatically expand hiring of educators and support staff.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: despite 82 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would authorize roughly $1.9 trillion over ten years for public schools and Bureau of Indian Education schools: grants to rebuild or retrofit school buildings into zero-carbon, contamination-free facilities, block grants to hire counselors, psychologists, nurses, teachers and other staff for ten years, $44 billion a year for special education, and $74 billion a year for high-poverty school funding. The poorest third of schools would get retrofit projects fully paid by the federal government. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in under-resourced schools, who would get smaller student-to-staff ratios, school psychologists, counselors, social workers, nurses, and buildings stripped of asbestos, lead, and mold with clean air and temperature control. School employees would gain jobs and prevailing-wage protections. Construction and renewable-energy workers in the communities would gain work under local-hiring, apprenticeship, and Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rules. Bureau of Indian Education schools would receive guaranteed funding with Tribal sovereignty protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and staff in under-resourced public schools

how_it_helps.text: Grants would cover 100 percent of the cost of converting the nation's most vulnerable third of schools into zero-carbon buildings with no asbestos, mold, lead, or PCBs, clean air, and full accessibility; middle- and least-vulnerable schools would get two-thirds and one-third coverage respectively.

Resource block grants would fund ten years of new full-time staff — including a target of one school counselor and one social worker per 250 students and one psychologist per 500 — plus raises and tuition support for paraprofessionals.
The bill would authorize $44 billion a year for IDEA special education and $74 billion a year for Title I high-poverty school funding, far above current appropriations.

Construction work would carry Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, registered apprenticeships making up at least 20 percent of crews, project labor agreements on large projects, and hiring preferences for local residents, veterans, and formerly incarcerated workers.
All Bureau of Indian Education schools would be fully funded for every grant program, with technical assistance and explicit Tribal sovereignty and self-determination protections.

At least half of the climate resiliency funds would go to environmental justice communities, for projects like electric school buses, backup power, flood protection, and universal high-speed internet for schools.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill authorizes about $1.9 trillion in appropriations over ten years — roughly $446 billion for building retrofits, $250 billion for staff hiring, $440 billion for IDEA, $740 billion for Title I, $44 billion for resiliency, and $100 million for equity planning — with no tax, offset, or revenue source identified anywhere in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through new borrowing or taxes

drawbacks.text: The cost is enormous: about $1.9 trillion in authorized spending over a decade, with no identified funding source, offset, or revenue provision anywhere in the bill's text.
School districts would have to commit to retaining all federally funded positions with their own money after the ten-year grant period ends, creating a fiscal cliff for local budgets.

The bill prescribes local programming in detail, requiring funded schools to teach Green New Deal principles, banning law-enforcement-based safety measures, and mandating union neutrality policies and project labor agreements — provisions critics would call federal overreach into locally governed schools and a boon to organized labor at the expense of non-union contractors.

It was written as a wish list rather than legislation that could pass: no hearing, no committee markup, and no cost estimate from the Congressional Budget Office ever occurred, so the real price and implementation burden were never examined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside for students and school workers is real and large — full federal funding of special education, one counselor per 250 students, and buildings free of lead and mold in the poorest districts. But the bill as written was not a serious attempt at legislation: it authorizes nearly $2 trillion with no way to pay for it, leaves school districts holding the bill for permanent staffing after ten years, and hard-codes ideological and labor provisions into construction contracts. Even a sympathetic Congress would have had to shrink and restructure it substantially before it could be responsibly enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or markup, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamaal Bowman, a former middle school principal, introduced the bill on September 28, 2023, with 82 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which was the last action the bill ever received.
The committee — led by Republicans in the 118th Congress — took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one in particular. Because the bill died without ever being debated or scored, students and school workers gained nothing, and taxpayers were never actually on the hook for the authorized spending either. The main effect was that its supporters made a public statement of goals.

for.name: Jamaal Bowman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Green New Deal for Public Schools Act and gathered 82 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 82 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Jayapal, Pressley, and Khanna
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a large bloc of support within the House Democratic caucus.

against.name: Virginia Foxx and the House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; no Republican cosponsored it, and no vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 83 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling the House and the committee, the bill never moved at all.

industries.industry: School construction and green retrofit contractors
industries.note: The bill would have steered hundreds of billions of dollars into converting school buildings to zero-carbon, contamination-free facilities, creating a decade-long pipeline of public construction work. Local-hiring preferences and prevailing-wage rules would have directed much of that work to community workers.

industries.industry: Organized labor (building trades and teacher unions)
industries.note: The bill requires project labor agreements on large projects, at least 20 percent registered apprentices, union neutrality policies, and full bargaining-unit status for federally funded school staff. It would have locked union labor into a massive new spending stream.

Every funded school would need onsite solar, batteries, and all-electric heating, cooling, and cooking, with Buy American sourcing rules — a large guaranteed market for solar installers and heat pump and battery manufacturers.

The bill bars building new schools within 2,500 feet of oil or gas wells and funds electrification that displaces fossil fuel heating and cooking in schools. The direct financial impact is modest since the bill never advanced.
